verses.text: This is the family of Reuben, Israel's firstborn. Reuben was the firstborn, but when he defiled his father's bed, his birthright went to the sons of Joseph son of Israel. So the family record doesn't list him according to that birthright.
Judah became stronger than his brothers, and a ruler came from him, but the birthright belonged to Joseph.
Reuben, Israel's firstborn, had four sons: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
Joel's family line continued through his son Shemaiah, then Gog and Shimei,
then Micah, Reaiah, and Baal,
and then Beerah. Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria took Beerah captive. He had been a leader of the Reubenites.
The records of his relatives by family listed Jeiel the chief, Zechariah,
and Bela son of Azaz, whose father was Shema son of Joel. Bela and his people lived at Aroer, as far as Nebo and Baal Meon.
They settled eastward as far as the edge of the wilderness leading toward the Euphrates, because their herds had grown so large in Gilead.
In Saul's time they fought the Hagrites and defeated them. They moved into their tents throughout the land east of Gilead.
Gad's descendants lived next to them in Bashan, as far as Salecah.
Joel was their chief, Shapham was second, and Janai and Shaphat also lived in Bashan.
Their relatives, by household, were Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia, and Eber, seven in all.
These were the descendants of Abihail son of Huri. His family line went back through Jaroah, Gilead, Michael, Jeshishai, Jahdo, and Buz.
Ahi son of Abdiel and grandson of Guni was the head of their families.
They lived in Gilead, in Bashan and its towns, and throughout the pasturelands of Sharon as far as their borders.
All these families were entered in the records in the days of King Jotham of Judah and King Jeroboam of Israel.

Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had forty-four thousand seven hundred and sixty men fit to go to war. They were brave fighters who could handle a shield and sword, shoot a bow, and fight skillfully.
They fought against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab.
They received help, and the Hagrites and their allies were handed over to them. They cried out to God in battle, and he answered because they trusted him.
They took fifty thousand camels, two hundred and fifty thousand sheep, and two thousand donkeys, and they took a hundred thousand people captive.
Many were killed because the battle was from God. The victors lived in their land until the exile.
The people of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land and grew numerous from Bashan to Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon.
Their family heads were Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel. They were brave warriors, well-known men who led their families.
But they were unfaithful to the God of their ancestors. They turned to the gods of the peoples God had destroyed before them.

So the God of Israel stirred up Pul king of Assyria and Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria. The Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh were taken captive to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan, where they remain to this day.
